about.p: A *collocation* is a pair or group of words that are often used together, such as *heavy rain*, *make a decision* or *highly unlikely*. Native speakers say *strong wind* but not *heavy wind*. Learning collocations makes your English sound natural and helps you to express ideas precisely.

Units 1–5 teach you how to find and record collocations and how they differ in register. Units 6–12 look at grammatical patterns (intensifying adverbs, everyday verbs) and special areas such as metaphor. The rest of the book presents collocations by topic and by function. Each **left-hand page** presents the collocations in texts and examples; the **right-hand page** practises them.

about.-: Learn each collocation as one unit: on every card the whole phrase is the item, with its meaning and an example.
*Complete the phrase* questions hide one word of the collocation and ask you to choose it: this is the book's main exercise, choosing the word that goes with another.
This course follows the second edition. Two first-edition units that are not in the second edition (Feelings and emotions, Computers) are added at the end.

about.tip: When you read in English, notice word partners and write them down as pairs: not *rain* but *heavy rain*, *torrential rain*, *the rain stopped*.

L.p: A collocation is a pair or group of words that are often used together. They sound natural to native speakers, but they are often hard to guess. We say *fast cars* and *fast food*, but *a quick glance* and *a quick meal* (not *a fast glance*).

Some collocations are fixed: only *take* goes with *a photo*. Others are more open: you can *keep to* or *stick to* the rules. A wrong collocation may be understood (*I did a few mistakes*) but sounds unnatural: say *I made a few mistakes*.
Collocations give you the most natural way to say something, more colourful or precise alternatives (*bitterly cold* instead of *very cold*) and a better style in writing (*poverty breeds crime*).

W: fast cars|col|cars that can go very quickly|He has always loved [fast cars].|A
fast food|col|hot food that is served quickly, like burgers|We stopped for some [fast food] on the motorway.|A
a {quick} glance|col|a very short look|She took [a quick glance] at her watch.|A
a {quick} meal|col|food eaten in a short time|We just had [a quick meal] before the film.|A
{take} a photo|col|use a camera to make a picture|Could you [take a photo] of us?|B
{keep} to the rules|col|obey the rules|Everyone must [keep to the rules].|B|also: stick to the rules
{make} an effort|col|try hard|You must [make an effort] to study for your exams.|B
{watch} TV|col|look at television programmes|Did you [watch TV] last night?|B
a {powerful} engine|col|an engine with a lot of power|This car has a very [powerful engine].|B
{ancient} monuments|col|very old historic buildings or structures|There are some [ancient monuments] near the village.|B
{make} a mistake|col|do something wrong|I [made a few mistakes] in the test.|B
{strictly} forbidden|col|completely not allowed|Smoking is [strictly forbidden] in the building.|C
{bitterly} cold|col|extremely cold|It was [bitterly cold] that night.|C
{pitch} dark|col|completely dark|By six o'clock it was [pitch dark].|C
poverty {breeds} crime|col|poverty causes crime|Many people believe that [poverty breeds crime].|C

L.p: Train yourself to notice collocations whenever you read or listen to English, and look them up in a good learner's dictionary. If you look up *sharp*, you will find *a sharp pain, a sharp bend, a sharp contrast, a sharp rise*.

Record a collocation in a phrase or sentence and highlight it: *Jim gave me a very useful piece of advice.* Revise regularly, use the collocations in sentences about your own life, and group them by topic or by key word.

L.e: I learnt the hard way that Jack can't be trusted. You must give way to traffic from the left.

a {sharp} bend|col|a sudden turn in a road|Slow down – there's [a sharp bend] ahead.|A

{ease} the pain|col|make pain less strong|A hot bath may [ease the pain].|A

units.O: Start a collocation notebook page. Choose one common word (way, time, make…) and write six collocations with it in example sentences.

L.p: A good learner's dictionary shows collocations in bold or in its examples. Look at some collocations of *pain*: you can *feel*, *suffer* or *experience* pain; things can *ease*, *relieve* or *soothe* the pain; someone can *inflict* pain; the pain *subsides*.
A dictionary also tells you if a collocation is formal or informal: *take someone up on an offer* is informal; *accept an offer* is neutral.

L.tip: When you look up a word, note at least two of its collocations, and check whether they are formal or informal.

{relieve} pain|col|make pain less severe|These tablets will [relieve the pain].|A

{constant} pain|col|pain that never stops|She was in [constant pain].|A

{accept} an offer|col|say yes to an offer|She [accepted] the job [offer].|B
a {kind} offer|col|a generous offer|That's a very [kind offer].|B

L.p: English has many ways to say *very*. Words like *highly, utterly, bitterly* and *deeply* collocate with particular words, and other combinations sound unnatural.
*Highly* goes with probability words (*highly unlikely*) and usually with positive words (*highly successful*), but also *highly controversial*.
Use *absolutely* and (more formal) *utterly* with extreme adjectives: *absolutely exhausted* (not *very exhausted*), but *very tired* (not *absolutely tired*).
